name: Quality of Questions Asked by the Teacher
definition: What kinds of questions the teacher asks, and whether they make children think. A closed question needs a yes/no or one-word answer, an open question needs a longer answer, and the strongest questions ask "why" and are followed up.
level_text: No questions asked by the teacher, or asks the questions but gives the answers without waiting for students to answer.
example: Teacher: "What is the capital of Pakistan? Islamabad. Write it down."

name: Quality of Questions Asked by the Teacher
definition: What kinds of questions the teacher asks, and whether they make children think. A closed question needs a yes/no or one-word answer, an open question needs a longer answer, and the strongest questions ask "why" and are followed up.
level_text: Teacher only asks closed questions with yes/no or one word answers.
example: Teacher: "Is a cow a mammal?" Student: "Yes."

name: Quality of Questions Asked by the Teacher
definition: What kinds of questions the teacher asks, and whether they make children think. A closed question needs a yes/no or one-word answer, an open question needs a longer answer, and the strongest questions ask "why" and are followed up.
level_text: Teacher asks at least two open questions and waits for students to answer.
example: Teacher: "Ali, how did you work that out?" (waits) Student: "I counted in twos."

name: Quality of Questions Asked by the Teacher
definition: What kinds of questions the teacher asks, and whether they make children think. A closed question needs a yes/no or one-word answer, an open question needs a longer answer, and the strongest questions ask "why" and are followed up.
level_text: Teacher asks at least one question using 'why' and then follows up on the same child's answer (why? how do you know?).
example: Teacher: "Why does a plant need water?" Student: "To grow." Teacher: "How do you know it helps it grow?"

name: Helping when a child is wrong
definition: What the teacher does when a child's answer is wrong or incomplete: ignores it, says it is wrong, explains why, or helps the child fix it. It only applies when an answer was actually wrong.
level_text: A student gives a wrong answer and the teacher ignores it, or only repeats the same explanation in the same words.
example: Student: "Seven." Teacher: "Next one."

name: Helping when a child is wrong
definition: What the teacher does when a child's answer is wrong or incomplete: ignores it, says it is wrong, explains why, or helps the child fix it. It only applies when an answer was actually wrong.
level_text: The teacher says the answer is wrong, or explains again, but gives the reason for the correction at most once.
example: Teacher: "No, that is wrong. It is nine."

name: Helping when a child is wrong
definition: What the teacher does when a child's answer is wrong or incomplete: ignores it, says it is wrong, explains why, or helps the child fix it. It only applies when an answer was actually wrong.
level_text: At least two times, the teacher gives the reason for the correction and says what was right and what to change.
example: Teacher: "Not quite. You counted the 4 twice, so it is 9, not 13."

name: Helping when a child is wrong
definition: What the teacher does when a child's answer is wrong or incomplete: ignores it, says it is wrong, explains why, or helps the child fix it. It only applies when an answer was actually wrong.
level_text: Beyond level 3, the teacher asks the student or another student to fix the answer, and tries a new way (a new example, a picture, smaller steps) if they are still stuck.
example: Teacher: "Ali, what do you do first?" ... "Still stuck? Let me show you with sticks."

name: Who got to answer
definition: How the teacher chooses who answers: only children who put a hand up or call out, or ways of bringing in other children, such as calling different children by name, pair talk, or everyone writing an answer.
level_text: The teacher asks the whole class and takes whoever answers. No way of choosing who answers is heard: no name called before the question, no talking in pairs, no "everyone write".
example: Teacher: "Who knows?" Student: "Me, me!" Teacher: "Yes, you."

name: Who got to answer
definition: How the teacher chooses who answers: only children who put a hand up or call out, or ways of bringing in other children, such as calling different children by name, pair talk, or everyone writing an answer.
level_text: The teacher uses a way of choosing who answers one time, for example calls a student by name, then goes back to taking whoever answers.
example: Teacher: "Sara, what is your answer?" ... then "Who knows?" for the rest of the lesson.

name: Who got to answer
definition: How the teacher chooses who answers: only children who put a hand up or call out, or ways of bringing in other children, such as calling different children by name, pair talk, or everyone writing an answer.
level_text: At least two times, the teacher uses a way of choosing who answers (a name called before the question, "tell your partner", "everyone write your answer", names picked at random).
example: Teacher: "Ali, what do you think?" ... later: "Everyone, tell your partner your answer." (two times: a name called, then pair talk)

name: Who got to answer
definition: How the teacher chooses who answers: only children who put a hand up or call out, or ways of bringing in other children, such as calling different children by name, pair talk, or everyone writing an answer.
level_text: Beyond level 3, the teacher calls at least two different names to answer, and each is followed by an answer.
example: Teacher: "Ali, what is seven plus five?" Student: "Twelve." ... later: Teacher: "Ayesha, what is nine plus six?" Student: "Fifteen." (two different names called before the question, each followed by an answer)

name: Children's choices
definition: Whether children have a say in how the lesson goes: a real choice about how to do the work or explain it, the teacher taking up a child's idea, or a part of the lesson handed to them. Small choices (who goes first, which colour) are not real choices.
level_text: The teacher decides everything and asks students for no choice or idea.
example: Teacher: "Open your copy. Write the date. Copy this sentence."

name: Children's choices
definition: Whether children have a say in how the lesson goes: a real choice about how to do the work or explain it, the teacher taking up a child's idea, or a part of the lesson handed to them. Small choices (who goes first, which colour) are not real choices.
level_text: The teacher lets students choose only small things (who goes first, which colour), and decides everything about the learning.
example: Teacher: "Which colour pen do you want to use?"

name: Children's choices
definition: Whether children have a say in how the lesson goes: a real choice about how to do the work or explain it, the teacher taking up a child's idea, or a part of the lesson handed to them. Small choices (who goes first, which colour) are not real choices.
level_text: The teacher gives students at least one real choice about how to do the work or how to explain it, and lets them follow it, or takes up a child's idea.
example: Teacher: "You can draw it or write it, you decide." / "Use any method you like." / Student: "Miss, can we draw it first?" Teacher: "Good idea, we will draw it first."

name: Children's choices
definition: Whether children have a say in how the lesson goes: a real choice about how to do the work or explain it, the teacher taking up a child's idea, or a part of the lesson handed to them. Small choices (who goes first, which colour) are not real choices.
level_text: Beyond level 3, the teacher hands a part of the lesson to students: a student or a group leads an activity, picks the method, or teaches the others.
example: Teacher: "Ali, come to the board and show everyone how you did it. We will do it Ali's way."

name: Switching activities
definition: How smoothly the class moves from one activity to the next: whether the teacher gives a clear signal and how long the change takes.
level_text: The class takes more than three minutes to change activity, and the teacher gives no clear signal.
example: Teacher: "Now... no, wait... take out your... everyone, listen... take out your copies." (more than three minutes pass)

name: Switching activities
definition: How smoothly the class moves from one activity to the next: whether the teacher gives a clear signal and how long the change takes.
level_text: The teacher gives a signal, but the change still takes two to three minutes.
example: Teacher: "Now group work." (the class is still moving chairs; group work starts about three minutes later)

name: Switching activities
definition: How smoothly the class moves from one activity to the next: whether the teacher gives a clear signal and how long the change takes.
level_text: The class changes activity in under two minutes of the teacher's signal.
example: Teacher: "Pens down, now turn to page 20." (the next activity starts at once; check the times)

name: Switching activities
definition: How smoothly the class moves from one activity to the next: whether the teacher gives a clear signal and how long the change takes.
level_text: Beyond level 3, students already know what comes next and change without being told.
example: Student: "Miss, is it group work now?" (they are already moving)

name: Safe to be wrong
definition: Whether children feel safe to try and be wrong: how the teacher responds to their answers, whether praise is for effort or only for right answers, and whether mistakes are treated as useful.
level_text: The teacher gives no encouragement. Replies to students are flat, dismissive, or only about the task.
example: Teacher: "Wrong. Sit down." / "Next."

name: Safe to be wrong
definition: Whether children feel safe to try and be wrong: how the teacher responds to their answers, whether praise is for effort or only for right answers, and whether mistakes are treated as useful.
level_text: The teacher praises, but only for right answers or for doing as told, and only in general words.
example: Teacher: "Good." / "Well done." (only after right answers)

name: Safe to be wrong
definition: Whether children feel safe to try and be wrong: how the teacher responds to their answers, whether praise is for effort or only for right answers, and whether mistakes are treated as useful.
level_text: At least two times, the teacher praises a student's effort, trying, or thinking, not just a right answer.
example: Teacher: "Good try, Ali, you were thinking the right way." / "Thank you for having a go."

name: Safe to be wrong
definition: Whether children feel safe to try and be wrong: how the teacher responds to their answers, whether praise is for effort or only for right answers, and whether mistakes are treated as useful.
level_text: Beyond level 3, the teacher treats a wrong answer or an attempt as useful, and also invites other views.
example: Teacher: "That is a good mistake, it shows us what to check. Does anyone see it differently?"

name: Group work
definition: Whether the teacher sets real pair or group work: a task the group can only finish together, with something to make, roles and a report back. Sitting together but working alone is not group work.
level_text: The teacher gives no pair or group task. Everyone works alone or as one class.

name: Group work
definition: Whether the teacher sets real pair or group work: a task the group can only finish together, with something to make, roles and a report back. Sitting together but working alone is not group work.
level_text: The teacher puts students in pairs or groups, but each student does their own work.
example: Teacher: "Sit in your groups. Each of you write the answer in your own copy."

name: Group work
definition: Whether the teacher sets real pair or group work: a task the group can only finish together, with something to make, roles and a report back. Sitting together but working alone is not group work.
level_text: The teacher gives a task that a group can only finish together, and says what the group must make.
example: Teacher: "In your group, make one chart together. Put everyone's ideas on it."

name: Group work
definition: Whether the teacher sets real pair or group work: a task the group can only finish together, with something to make, roles and a report back. Sitting together but working alone is not group work.
level_text: Beyond level 3, the teacher gives roles or turns inside the group, and asks the group to report back.
example: Teacher: "One of you is the writer, one is the speaker. Each group will tell us what you found."

name: Books and materials
definition: Whether books, the board, charts or objects are used for learning, and by whom: only shown by the teacher, used by the children, or used by a child to explain while the teacher builds on what the child says.
level_text: The teacher never mentions a book, the board, a chart, or any object or picture.

name: Books and materials
definition: Whether books, the board, charts or objects are used for learning, and by whom: only shown by the teacher, used by the children, or used by a child to explain while the teacher builds on what the child says.
level_text: The teacher mentions a book, the board, or an object only to show or tell, and does not ask students to use it.
example: Teacher: "Look at the board." / "I will show you with these sticks."

name: Books and materials
definition: Whether books, the board, charts or objects are used for learning, and by whom: only shown by the teacher, used by the children, or used by a child to explain while the teacher builds on what the child says.
level_text: The teacher asks students to use a book, the board, or an object themselves, and says how it connects to the idea.
example: Teacher: "Open your book to page 12 and find the picture of the plant. See, the roots are at the bottom."

name: Books and materials
definition: Whether books, the board, charts or objects are used for learning, and by whom: only shown by the teacher, used by the children, or used by a child to explain while the teacher builds on what the child says.
level_text: Beyond level 3, the teacher asks a student to explain with the book, the chart or the object, and builds on what the student says.
example: Teacher: "Ali, take the paper and show us one quarter." Student: "I cut it in four parts and coloured one." Teacher: "One part of four, yes. Now show us two quarters."

name: Children's reasoning
definition: How deep children's answers are: one word, a longer answer that only repeats what was said, or an answer that shows reasoning in the child's own words (says why, compares, uses a rule on a new case, explains a choice, gives their own example).
level_text: Students give only one-word answers or repeat a fact.
example: Student: "Twelve."

name: Children's reasoning
definition: How deep children's answers are: one word, a longer answer that only repeats what was said, or an answer that shows reasoning in the child's own words (says why, compares, uses a rule on a new case, explains a choice, gives their own example).
level_text: At least one answer, from any student, is longer than a phrase, but it only repeats what was already said or read, or finishes the teacher's sentence.
example: Teacher: "Because they were very small, they thought that..." Student: "...my going to the earth is useless."

name: Children's reasoning
definition: How deep children's answers are: one word, a longer answer that only repeats what was said, or an answer that shows reasoning in the child's own words (says why, compares, uses a rule on a new case, explains a choice, gives their own example).
level_text: At least two answers, from any students, show reasoning in the child's own words: they say why, compare two things, use a rule on a new case, or explain a choice. Finishing the teacher's sentence, or repeating a reason the teacher already gave, does not count.
example: Teacher: "Why 210, why not 150?" Student: "Because we subtracted 150 from the complete angle."

name: Children's reasoning
definition: How deep children's answers are: one word, a longer answer that only repeats what was said, or an answer that shows reasoning in the child's own words (says why, compares, uses a rule on a new case, explains a choice, gives their own example).
level_text: Beyond level 3, a student gives their own example, or links the idea to something else, that the teacher did not say first.
example: Teacher: "How does a dream get shattered?" Student: "If I had a project and it broke, my dream was shattered." / Teacher: "What is urbanisation?" Student: "The school being built now, it affected the ecosystem."

name: How many children spoke
definition: How many different children speak across the lesson, and whether children silent early on speak later.
level_text: No student speaks during the lesson.

name: How many children spoke
definition: How many different children speak across the lesson, and whether children silent early on speak later.
level_text: Only the same one or two children speak.
example: (coach) "Only Ali and Sara answered all lesson; 30 student turns, almost all theirs."

name: How many children spoke
definition: How many different children speak across the lesson, and whether children silent early on speak later.
level_text: Three to five different children speak.
example: (coach) "4 different children answered, all from the front rows."

name: How many children spoke
definition: How many different children speak across the lesson, and whether children silent early on speak later.
level_text: Six or more different children speak, and at least two children who had not spoken in the first half speak in the second half.
example: (coach) "9 different children spoke, including 2 from the back row who were quiet until the group activity."

name: Children answering each other
definition: Whether children talk to each other about the task, not only to the teacher: one child answers, agrees with or adds to what another said. At its strongest they give reasons to agree or disagree and reach one shared answer.
level_text: No student speaks to another student about the task.
example: Student: "Is the answer twelve, miss?" Teacher: "Yes, it is twelve." (the teacher answered, so the student was talking to the teacher)

name: Children answering each other
definition: Whether children talk to each other about the task, not only to the teacher: one child answers, agrees with or adds to what another said. At its strongest they give reasons to agree or disagree and reach one shared answer.
level_text: One time, a student answers and the teacher names a second child who agrees with the previous student's answer, or the student says I agree with her/him referring to the previously given answer by the student.
example: Teacher: "Ali, what is your answer?" Student: "Twelve." Teacher: "Hina, do you agree?" Student: "Yes, it is twelve." (the teacher names a second child, who agrees) / Student: "It is twelve." Student: "I agree with him." (a child agrees with the answer just given)

name: Children answering each other
definition: Whether children talk to each other about the task, not only to the teacher: one child answers, agrees with or adds to what another said. At its strongest they give reasons to agree or disagree and reach one shared answer.
level_text: At least two times, a student answers, agrees with, or adds to what another student just said.
example: Teacher: "Sara, what is nine plus six?" Student: "Fifteen." Teacher: "Omar, do you agree?" Student: "Yes, it is fifteen." ... later: Student: "It is a verb." Student: "I agree with her."

name: Children answering each other
definition: Whether children talk to each other about the task, not only to the teacher: one child answers, agrees with or adds to what another said. At its strongest they give reasons to agree or disagree and reach one shared answer.
level_text: Beyond level 3, students give a reason to agree or disagree with each other, and reach one shared answer. N/A  Do not score this indicator if there are no two Student lines in a row where students talk about the topic, and the teacher never names a second child to agree with a student's answer. It is then left out of the feedback.
example: Student: "It is a noun because we can see it." Student: "No, it is a verb because it shows an action." Student: "Okay, so it is a verb, we agree."

name: Trying when unsure
definition: Whether children dare to answer when they are not sure: they stay silent, answer only when sure, answer while unsure, or answer unasked and try again after a wrong answer. Only the trying counts, not whether the answer is right.
level_text: When the teacher asks, students stay silent, say "I do not know", or wait for the teacher to give the answer.

name: Trying when unsure
definition: Whether children dare to answer when they are not sure: they stay silent, answer only when sure, answer while unsure, or answer unasked and try again after a wrong answer. Only the trying counts, not whether the answer is right.
level_text: Students answer only when they are sure. Nobody gives a half-sure answer; when unsure they say nothing.

name: Trying when unsure
definition: Whether children dare to answer when they are not sure: they stay silent, answer only when sure, answer while unsure, or answer unasked and try again after a wrong answer. Only the trying counts, not whether the answer is right.
level_text: At least two times, a student answers while clearly unsure, for example "Maybe...", "Should I say...?", or an answer that changes halfway.
example: Teacher: "What is seven plus five?" Student: "Maybe it is... twelve." ... later: Teacher: "Which word is the verb?" Student: "Should I say... the second one?" ... later: Teacher: "What is nine plus six?" Student: "Fourteen... no, wait, fifteen." (three times, one of each cue)

name: Trying when unsure
definition: Whether children dare to answer when they are not sure: they stay silent, answer only when sure, answer while unsure, or answer unasked and try again after a wrong answer. Only the trying counts, not whether the answer is right.
level_text: Beyond level 3, a student answers without being asked, or tries again after a wrong answer instead of giving up.
example: Student: "Miss, I want to try." / (after "No") Student: "Wait, then it is fourteen."

name: Children's own questions
definition: Whether children ask questions of their own: only about the task (which page, may I answer), or about the idea itself (how or why something works, a different case). Repeating the teacher's question or giving an unsure answer does not count.
level_text: No student asks the teacher a question of their own. An unsure answer ("Is it twelve?") or a student repeating the teacher's question ("Why?") does not count.

name: Children's own questions
definition: Whether children ask questions of their own: only about the task (which page, may I answer), or about the idea itself (how or why something works, a different case). Repeating the teacher's question or giving an unsure answer does not count.
level_text: Students ask only questions about the task: which page, do we write this, is it homework, may I answer, or please say it again.
example: Student: "Which page, miss?" / "May I answer?" / "Sorry, what?"

name: Children's own questions
definition: Whether children ask questions of their own: only about the task (which page, may I answer), or about the idea itself (how or why something works, a different case). Repeating the teacher's question or giving an unsure answer does not count.
level_text: Students ask at least one question about the idea itself: how or why something works, or what would happen in a different case.
example: Student: "Why does the answer get bigger?" / "What if we use five instead of three?"

name: Children's own questions
definition: Whether children ask questions of their own: only about the task (which page, may I answer), or about the idea itself (how or why something works, a different case). Repeating the teacher's question or giving an unsure answer does not count.
level_text: Beyond level 3, students ask at least two questions about the idea, and one of them is about something the teacher has not talked about in this lesson.
example: (lesson on adding) Student: "Can we add numbers bigger than a million?"

name: Accuracy of content
definition: Whether what the teacher says about the subject is correct, and whether a wrong statement is corrected. Count something as wrong only when you are sure.
level_text: The teacher says something wrong and leaves it, so students are left with wrong information. Count something as wrong only if you are sure; a word that may be a transcription or translation mistake does not count.
example: Teacher: "A spider is an insect. It has six legs." (a spider has eight legs)

name: Accuracy of content
definition: Whether what the teacher says about the subject is correct, and whether a wrong statement is corrected. Count something as wrong only when you are sure.
level_text: Mostly correct, but the teacher makes a small slip (a wrong rule or a wrong word) and does not correct it.
example: Teacher: "The bottom number is the numerator." (it is the denominator; nobody corrects it)

name: Accuracy of content
definition: Whether what the teacher says about the subject is correct, and whether a wrong statement is corrected. Count something as wrong only when you are sure.
level_text: Everything the teacher says is correct. When not sure, the teacher says so and does not guess.
example: Teacher: "I am not sure about that date. Let us check the book."

name: Accuracy of content
definition: Whether what the teacher says about the subject is correct, and whether a wrong statement is corrected. Count something as wrong only when you are sure.
level_text: Beyond level 3, the teacher warns students about a common mistake before they make it.
example: Teacher: "Careful: many children add the bottom numbers too. We keep the bottom number the same."

name: Subject words
definition: Whether the teacher uses the subject's own words (such as "numerator" or "verb") and explains them, and whether children are made to use them.
level_text: The teacher uses everyday words only, and no subject words.
example: Teacher: "Take away three." (never "subtract")

name: Subject words
definition: Whether the teacher uses the subject's own words (such as "numerator" or "verb") and explains them, and whether children are made to use them.
level_text: The teacher uses some subject words but does not explain them, or mixes them up.
example: Teacher: "Find the sum." ... "Now the total." ... "Now the answer." (the same thing, three words, none explained)

name: Subject words
definition: Whether the teacher uses the subject's own words (such as "numerator" or "verb") and explains them, and whether children are made to use them.
level_text: At least two times, the teacher uses a subject word and explains what it means.
example: Teacher: "The numerator is the top number. It tells us how many parts we have."

name: Subject words
definition: Whether the teacher uses the subject's own words (such as "numerator" or "verb") and explains them, and whether children are made to use them.
level_text: Beyond level 3, the teacher makes students use the subject words, and corrects loose words by giving the right one.
example: Student: "The bottom number." Teacher: "We say denominator. Say it."

name: Explaining why
definition: Whether the teacher explains why a rule or step works, with a reason, an example or a picture, or only says how to do it. At its strongest, the teacher turns a child's question into a short lesson or asks the children to give the reason.
level_text: The teacher only says how to do it, and gives no reason.
example: Teacher: "First add, then divide. Do it this way."

name: Explaining why
definition: Whether the teacher explains why a rule or step works, with a reason, an example or a picture, or only says how to do it. At its strongest, the teacher turns a child's question into a short lesson or asks the children to give the reason.
level_text: The teacher gives a reason now and then, but mostly asks students to remember the rule.
example: Teacher: "Just remember: a noun is a naming word."

name: Explaining why
definition: Whether the teacher explains why a rule or step works, with a reason, an example or a picture, or only says how to do it. At its strongest, the teacher turns a child's question into a short lesson or asks the children to give the reason.
level_text: At least two times, the teacher explains why a rule or step works, with a reason, an example, or a picture.
example: Teacher: "We keep the bottom number the same because the parts are the same size. Look at the picture."

name: Explaining why
definition: Whether the teacher explains why a rule or step works, with a reason, an example or a picture, or only says how to do it. At its strongest, the teacher turns a child's question into a short lesson or asks the children to give the reason.
level_text: Beyond level 3, the teacher turns a student's question into a short lesson that goes further, or asks the children to give the reason.
example: Student: "Why is it a verb?" Teacher: "Good question. Let us test it together..." / Teacher: "We keep the bottom number the same. Why? Who can tell us the reason?" Student: "Because the parts are the same size."

name: Links to real life
definition: Whether the teacher links the lesson to real life, another subject or an earlier lesson, with an example or comparison, and explains the link. At its strongest, children build on the teacher's link.
level_text: The teacher gives no real-life example, comparison, or link to another subject or an earlier lesson.

name: Links to real life
definition: Whether the teacher links the lesson to real life, another subject or an earlier lesson, with an example or comparison, and explains the link. At its strongest, children build on the teacher's link.
level_text: The teacher mentions a link and moves on without explaining it.
example: Teacher: "This is like shopping. Now back to the page."

name: Links to real life
definition: Whether the teacher links the lesson to real life, another subject or an earlier lesson, with an example or comparison, and explains the link. At its strongest, children build on the teacher's link.
level_text: The teacher gives a link and explains how it fits the idea.
example: Teacher: "If you buy three pens at five rupees each, you pay three fives. That is multiplication."

name: Links to real life
definition: Whether the teacher links the lesson to real life, another subject or an earlier lesson, with an example or comparison, and explains the link. At its strongest, children build on the teacher's link.
level_text: Beyond level 3, a student builds on the teacher's link: they add to it, ask about it, or explain it in their own words.
example: Teacher: "Three pens at five rupees each: you pay three fives." Student: "And if I buy four pens, I pay four fives, so twenty."
